A name and a nickname
2 January, 9:00 in Bucharest (16:00 in Hiroshima). A video call with Haruka and Sakura, who is on winter break. Ana and Mihai have news: on New Year’s Eve they chose their daughter’s name.
Big brother, big sister, Happy New Year!
Happy New Year, Sakura! Here’s to another good year together.
Happy New Year. Ana, how are you feeling? Are you all right after the false alarm?
Yes, I’m fine. Actually, we have some news today. The baby’s name has been decided.
What, really?! What is it? What is it?
On New Year’s Eve, the two of us decided to call her “Rosa Elena”.
Rosa Elena… what a lovely name. What does it mean?
Rosa comes from my grandmother, Rosario. Elena from Mihai’s mother. We decided to take both their names.
Rosario… the one with the wedding dress.
(After a short silence) …So it’s not a Japanese name.
Sorry, Sakura. We thought about Japanese names too, but…
No, it’s fine. It’s just that I kept thinking of Japanese names. I wrote ten of them in my notebook.
Then let’s do this: everyone in Japan will call her by a nickname you choose. What do you say?
Really?! …Well, Rosa is a flower, right? And Sakura is a flower too. So… “Hana-chan”!
Hana-chan. How cute.
Hana-chan…! That’s settled. Let’s agree: everyone in Japan calls her “Hana-chan”.
Yay! That means I gave her a name too!
Mihai, what about work? Once she’s born, you’ll both be busy.
I’ve decided to take a month off. I talked it over with the head of department, Ionescu, and he said “Of course”…
So it’s been arranged that I can be off from 10 January.
Good. Once a baby is born, there’s no time left for sleep.
That’s why I’ve made it a habit to sing your lullaby every evening. Though I still sing it badly.
Big brother, sing it! Now!
(Blushing) …Let’s save that for after Hana-chan is born.

ko-to ni su-ru / ko-to ni na-ru: the three words run together in one string, with no pause: “kotonisuru”. The “u” in “suru” is barely heard.
oo-mi-so-ka: a long “o” at the start (おお), then short, even syllables. Don’t confuse it with みそ (soybean paste).

ro-sa e-re-na: Japanese has no “l”, so “Elena” becomes エレナ with the light Japanese r. “Rosa” is ロサ (not “roza”): Japanese writes foreign names the way they sound in their own language (in Spanish the s is a real s).
1. ～こと に する: “I decide to…”
こと turns the verb into a noun (“the fact of…”), and に する means “to choose”. Together: “I choose the fact of…” = I DECIDE to. It’s a decision made by YOU (or by you and others), by your own will.
I decide (now)
I’m deciding to take a month off.
I’ve decided to take a month off.
We decided to take their names.
I decide NOT to
I’m deciding to stop eating sweets.
Let’s decide to call her “Hana-chan”.
Watch the tense: こと に した (past) = the decision has already been made and you’re announcing it. こと に する (present) = you’re making it right now, on the spot, like Mihai: …よぶ こと に する。どう?

You already learned noun + に する in ch. 19 (これ に します! = “I’ll have this!”). Now you put a verb instead of the noun, with こと in between: なまえ は ロサ エレナ に する (I choose a name) → ロサ エレナ に する こと に した (I decided to choose Rosa Elena).
2. ～こと に なる: “it’s been decided that… (not by me)”

With なる (“to become”) instead of する, the decision no longer comes from you: others made it, the company, the hospital, circumstances. Literally: “it has become the case that…”. Ionescu approved → やすめる こと に なりました (“it was arranged that I can be off”).
する (I decide)
なる (it’s been decided)
I decided to take a month.
It was arranged that I get a month off.
I decided to move to Bucharest.
I’m going to move to Bucharest (that’s how it was decided).

The Japanese also use こと に なりました for their own decisions, out of MODESTY: けっこん する こと に なりました (“it has come about that we’re getting married”) sounds humbler than けっこん する こと に しました. It’s the style of official announcements and letters.
A second meaning, in everyday speech: “that means…, it turns out that…”. Sakura: わたし も なまえ を つけた こと に なる ね! (“That means I gave her a name too!”). Like in English: “so technically, I named her!”.
3. ～こと に して いる vs ～こと に なって いる
With ～て いる (an ongoing state), the two forms describe what is ALWAYS true, not a one-off decision.
PERSONAL habit, rule
I make a point of singing every evening.
rule, schedule, custom SET by others
In Spain it’s customary to eat 12 grapes.
fixed schedule
Kenji is due to arrive on the 9th (that’s the schedule).
But we agreed that the two of us would choose the name.
Don’t swap them: ✗ スペイン で は ぶどう を たべる こと に して いる sounds as if the whole of Spain had personally decided it. A country’s custom, a hospital’s rule, a flight schedule → こと に なって いる.
4. こと に する, つもり, よてい: decision, intention, plan
In ch. 30 you learned つもり (intention) and よてい (plan). The difference from こと に する is the moment: こと に する stresses the MOMENT of deciding, the change “from now on”.
What it stresses
the intention in my head
いっかげつ やすむ つもり です。(I intend to)
a plan put in the calendar
とおか から やすむ よてい です。(it’s scheduled)
I made the decision (after thinking it over)
いっかげつ やすむ こと に しました。(I’ve decided)
it was decided (by others / by circumstances)
とおか から やすめる こと に なりました。(it was arranged)
English makes the same distinction: “I intend to…” (つもり), “it’s scheduled to…” (よてい), “I’ve decided to…” (こと に した), “it’s been decided that…” (こと に なった).
5. Culture: how names are given in Japan

In Japan, a child’s name is usually chosen with great care, based on the MEANING of the kanji: 花 (hana, flower), 桜 (sakura, cherry blossom), 陽 (hi, sun). Many families write the name beautifully on a sheet of paper and hang it on the wall or above the family altar on the SEVENTH day after the birth (おしちや, “the seventh night”), with a small family celebration. The name must be officially registered at the town hall within 14 days of the birth.

Foreign names are written in katakana, by sound: ロサ エレナ. Among friends and in the family, the Japanese add ～ちゃん for children and girls (はなちゃん, サクラちゃん), and ～くん for boys. An あだな (nickname) is very often a shortened name + ちゃん.

Just as in English “Elizabeth” becomes “Liz” or “Beth”, the Japanese make short forms from long names: ひなた → ひなちゃん. Sakura went one step further: she TRANSLATED the name into Japanese (Rosa = flower = はな).

おおみそか の なまえ — The name from New Year’s Eve
On the morning of New Year’s Eve, a long sheet of paper was stuck on the fridge door: the list of names for the baby.
More than twenty names were written on it, but almost all of them had been crossed out.
Ana and Mihai had decided that only the two of them would choose the name.
They also had a rule: they had decided to choose a name that could be said in Spanish, in Romanian and in Japanese.
That’s why Romanian names with “ș” or “ț” and Spanish names with “j” had all been crossed out.
But in those days, there were two grandmothers in the house every day.
One morning a new name had appeared at the bottom of the list: “Carmen”. It was in Carmen’s handwriting.
The next day, underneath it, was “Elena”. This time in Elena’s handwriting.
Mihai laughed: “But we agreed that we would choose the name.”
Carmen said “It’s just an idea”, and Elena “I didn’t write anything”, but both their eyes were smiling.
Towards evening, Elena came with sarmale. Carmen set out on the table grapes she had brought from Spain.
“In Spain it’s customary to eat twelve grapes along with the chimes of the clock at midnight.”
“One grape for each month. With each grape you make a wish.”
When Mihai translated, Elena’s eyes went wide. “Twelve? Can I really eat that fast?”
Around eight, Grandpa called from the village. Apparently he had borrowed the neighbours’ phone.
“Has the name been decided? I’ve made up my mind not to interfere. Just one thing.”
“A name is the first gift parents give their child. Give her the name of someone you love most of all.”
After hanging up, Mihai looked out of the window in silence for a while.
After dinner, Carmen took an old photograph out of her bag.
A young woman was standing in a garden full of roses.
“This is my mother, Rosario. She loved roses, and every morning she talked to the flowers in the garden.”
Ana looked at the photo and remembered the summers of her childhood.
“Grandma always used to say: ‘A rose has thorns, but it blooms in any weather. It’s a strong flower.’”
“She died when I was twelve, but when I wore her dress at my wedding, I felt as if we had met again.”
Elena, though she didn’t understand the words, looked at the photo for a long time and placed her hand on Ana’s.
Mihai and Ana went into the next room and talked in whispers.
“What about Rosa?” “I was just thinking the same thing.”
“Then the second one…” They both said the same name: “Elena”.
They say “Elena” means “light” in Greek. Ever since Mihai was little, Elena had always been the light of the house.
“Rosa is a strong flower, Elena is light. A rose that blooms in the light,” said Ana, and Mihai nodded: “That’s the one.”
Shortly before midnight, Mrs Doina and Mr Petre came too, with champagne.
When the clock struck on TV, everyone hurriedly ate their grapes.
Carmen ate hers skilfully, Elena with her mouth full, and Mrs Doina burst out laughing halfway through.
“What did you wish for?” Carmen asked, and Elena answered: “All twelve, for the baby.” Carmen laughed: “Me too.”
Outside, fireworks went up. Ana took Mihai by the hand and they stood up in front of everyone.
“We have an announcement for you all. We’ve decided the baby’s name will be ‘Rosa Elena’.”
Ana said it in Spanish, Mihai in Romanian. For a moment the room went quiet.
Then Carmen and Elena both burst into tears.
They hugged; Carmen kept saying “Gracias”, Elena “Mulțumesc”. Different words, the same meaning.
Mrs Doina was overjoyed: “Rosa Elena! Wonderful! I’ll call her ‘Rozița’!”
Carmen went to the fridge and crossed out “Carmen” on the list herself. Elena, laughing, drew a big circle next to “Elena”.
Late that night, Mihai handed Ana an envelope. “A present from me.”
Inside was a paper from the hospital. It said: “One month’s leave, from 10 January”.
“I talked to Dr Ionescu at the end of the year and decided to take time off. Her first month only happens once.”
“And what did Dr Ionescu say?” “‘Even a month is a bit short.’ In Romania fathers are entitled to take leave too.”
“But what about translating the manual?” “I’ve decided to finish all of it before the birth. I’m doing a little every evening.”
Without a word, Ana threw her arms around Mihai. Inside her belly, Rosa Elena gave a kick.
“See, it’s as if she already knows her name,” Ana laughed.
Outside, the fireworks could still be heard. It was the first night of the new year.
The next morning, the very first thing Mihai did was call the village. “Grandpa, it’s decided: Rosa Elena.”
At the other end, Grandpa said nothing for a long time. Then he said softly: “A beautiful name. Ileana is happy too.”
They decided to tell the family in Japan on the 2nd, by video. They were a little worried about what Sakura would say.
“Sakura must have wanted a Japanese name,” said Ana, and Mihai replied: “We’ll think about it when the time comes.”
